title: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

subtopics: CORS as a browser access policy, not authentication
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS).
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS), including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 6: HTTP, Browser Boundaries, and Transport Security. It builds practical understanding of Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) helps you observe a real boundary instead of assuming that browser, proxy, transport, and server behavior are interchangeable. Use a narrow, explicit origin allowlist based on the actual browser client; credentialed CORS requires careful origin handling and does not replace server-side authorization.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) can be understood through this sequence: Identify browser origin → Understand credentials → Narrow cross-origin policy → Test expected requests. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 42.1 CORS request and response headers; 42.2 Simple requests and preflight requests; 42.3 Explicit allowed-origin lists; 42.4 Credentialed requests; 42.5 Misconfiguration and excessive origin trust; 42.6 CORS as a browser access policy, not authentication. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Use a narrow, explicit origin allowlist based on the actual browser client; credentialed CORS requires careful origin handling and does not replace server-side authorization.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
content_blocks.expected_output: Only the listed frontend origin is allowed by this example; configure the production origin list separately.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Illustrative FastAPI configuration. Do not combine credentialed requests with a permissive wildcard origin; CORS is not authorization.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Use a narrow, explicit origin allowlist based on the actual browser client; credentialed CORS requires careful origin handling and does not replace server-side authorization. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Use a narrow, explicit origin allowlist based on the actual browser client; credentialed CORS requires careful origin handling and does not replace server-side authorization.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
